text: Walk into almost any large enterprise and you'll find cloud workloads sitting right next to a data center that's been running for decades, connected by VPNs and dedicated circuits, with identity systems spanning both. That's not an unfinished migration — for most organizations, that blend is the architecture. This lesson is about why enterprises actually end up hybrid, because the reasons determine which parts of that estate are temporary and which parts are structural, permanent facts you need to design around.

Four forces produce this, usually at the same time. Legacy systems are often too costly or too risky to migrate — the business case has to stand on its own, and for a system that already works, it frequently loses. Data residency and latency requirements are legal and physical constraints that cloud maturity never resolves. Mergers and acquisitions hand you another organization's entire estate on day one, on legal's timeline, not architecture's. And even a genuine cloud-first strategy executes in waves over years, so the 'temporary' hybrid middle of that migration often outlasts the original plan by a wide margin.

Here's what that looks like as a real decision instead of an accident: an architecture decision record for a nineteen-year-old scheduling system, with no remaining in-house expertise to rewrite it and downtime risk the business won't accept. The decision is to keep it on-premises indefinitely and connect it to the cloud ERP over a dedicated circuit rather than the public internet. The consequence is stated plainly — hybrid connectivity becomes a permanent requirement, not a step on the way to somewhere else.

The same four forces can produce two very different results. Accidental hybrid looks like ad hoc VPNs stitched together under deadline pressure, duplicated identity systems nobody fully owns, and no single team responsible for the boundary between on-prem and cloud. Designed hybrid starts from the same forces but adds governed connectivity, one identity model spanning both sides, and an explicit, revisited list of what stays and what moves. The forces don't change — whether anyone actually architected the outcome does.

That's the foundation for the rest of this chapter: treat hybrid as a durable fact of enterprise IT, not a waypoint you're racing to eliminate. Next lesson looks at the real connectivity patterns that join on-premises environments to the cloud — VPN and ExpressRoute or Direct Connect linking networks, and extending Active Directory into cloud identity — so that hybrid estate actually functions as one coherent architecture instead of two separate worlds bolted together.
